newsitem.title: SPAIN: FEATURE - Spanish fiestas stir animal groups into fury.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Spanish fiestas stir animal groups into fury.

text.p: Laughing youths hurl Marcela the goat from a church tower amid frenzied chants and cheers.
On the same day, a pig has its throat slit and is left to die before being made into sausages as revellers look on at a festival in the northern town of Burgo de Osma.
This year, geese hanging from rope will be decapitated by charging horsemen. Bulls, calves and pigs will be driven into the sea and other bulls will have their horns set on fire.
These are just a few of the rituals at Spanish fiestas that outrage animal rights activists.

"There are no cultural excuses for this sort of treatment of animals...It's a gratuitous spectacle and something that should be relegated to the history books where it belongs," said Jonathan Owen, spokesman for the World Society for the Protection of Animals.
"It's horrifying that these festivals are usually closely bound to the church...taking place on religious festivals and often on church property," he added.
Owen has appealed to the Vatican to intervene, but with little success.
"The pope should call an end to this abuse or at least make clear the Catholic Church wants no part of it, as such events go against the Catholic faith," said Owen.
But festival revellers fiercely defend their rituals and say outsiders should mind their own business.

"These are our traditions and there is nothing wrong with them," said Gerardo Castenero, a resident from Villanueva de la Vera which parades a donkey through its streets with the heaviest villager astride as the centrepiece of its fiesta.
"There are no problems with the animals and we love them and treat them well. People have no right telling us what we should do."
NO NATIONAL ANIMAL PROTECTION BILL
Despite promises to the contrary, Spain has no animal protection bill that covers the whole country.

"We have no hope for a national law because our government is not interested in this issue and for them animals are not important," said Eva Vallejo, spokeswoman for Spain's National Association for the Defence of Animals.
"But we are still asking why we haven't got a national law," she added.
The government says the responsibility to impose regulations lies with regional authorities.
Animal groups celebrated a minor victory in Madrid last summer when the regional government introduced laws to banish animal abuse during fiestas.
Madrid has subsequently begun actions against a number of villages which could face fines of up to 10 million pesetas ($69,000).
While other regions have introduced similar legislation, in reality such laws are not adhered to as closely and local authorites have failed to stamp out abuse.
The remote northern village of Manganeses de la Polvorosa is a perfect example, animal rights groups say.
Each year residents throw a goat from the local belfry into a canvas sheet held up by villagers below during the "Jump of the Goat" festival held in honour of their patron saint.
The "goat throwing" was officially banned in 1992 by the governor of Zamora province after fierce protests from animal groups and the media.
But villagers reacted so violently when police tried to stop the ceremony that the mayor was forced to rethink the ban.
A year later, villagers compromised and carried out a "goat-lowering" ceremony, easing the animal down on a rope.
This year villagers brushed aside any compromise and threw it the full 50 feet from the top of the belfry.
The newly appointed mayor denied that it had suffered and said tossing the goat instead of lowering it was less cruel.
"We throw the goat because it's better for the animal...It suffers less and spends less time in the air," said Demetrio Prieto.
Locals denounced animal groups' cries of foul play.
"No-one is going to take this tradition away from us," said villager Maria Jose Veleda.
GORY TRADITIONS PERSIST
Gruesome fiestas in other areas have also persisted.
In the northern village of Tordesillas, cockerels are hung upside down and slashed to death by blindfolded girls armed with swords, also in honour of their patron saint.
In the Levante region, a number of fiestas centre on a crazed bull whose horns are set on fire after being covered in hot wax or some other flammable substance.
Despite such goings on, animal rights activists are confident that attitudes are changing in Spain.

"There are encouraging signs because increasingly among the younger generation of Spaniards, especially those who don't live in rural areas, there is a growing feeling that they don't want these sorts of things happening any more," said Owen.

Such a change was illustrated by police in the Basque region who banned target practice on live goats for fear that it was damaging their image. According to police data, 19 goats had been killed over a 16-year period to study the effect of bullets on the body.
Animal activists are confident the government will move toward their way of thinking.
"The government is coming around...It is a member of the European Union and pressure through publicity and public opinion can have quite an influence on politicians," said Owen.
